The map for the next few slides: CSVs in, pandas shapes them, Altair draws them, marimo makes it interactive and turns it into these slides. Then we go through each step in code.
Ingestion: one tab per source system - click through them; the code underneath changes with the tab. The readings only name their sensor; the sensors tab says which plant each one is in.

Click: the data model, as a star schema. Facts in blue: the sensor readings, the grid settlement, and daily_plant_performance - one row per plant per day, what the dashboard is built on. Dimensions in lavender: sensors and plants. A reading only names its sensor; the sensor dimension says which plant it is in.
Raw sensors lie: a stuck value repeats, a dropout is NaN. Point at the shaded hours; the mint line is what we put there - the typical value for that hour over the nearby days.
Gold: hourly readings become daily energy, joined to what the grid operator paid - and self-consumption falls out as the difference.
Plotting, step 1: the simplest possible Altair chart - x, y, colour.
Step 2: lines become stacked areas.
Step 3: titles, outline, smooth curves, readable numbers.
Step 4: tooltips - hover the chart.

Step 3: marimo has no date-range slider, so the dashboard uses its own widget - an anywidget: a Python class with a small JavaScript front end and synced state. Defined once, used like any marimo element.

Four services really, dressed up nine ways.
Click through a tab or two live.
The three questions of the talk. The map is the plan for the rest of it: we go through it piece by piece, and every question mark becomes an open-source tool.
The map again, one piece at a time. First: getting the raw data in.

Airbyte copies data in: hundreds of open-source connectors, set up in a UI - pick a source, a destination and a schedule. Incremental syncs and CDC, so each run only moves what changed. For an API without a connector, the Connector Builder makes one without code. Click the dots to flip through the screenshots.
Storage: first how the data sits in files - Parquet, then the table formats on top - then the databases.

Parquet in one slide: a columnar, compressed file format for tables, from Twitter and Cloudera in 2013, after Google's Dremel paper. Great for analytics and data lakes; not for changing single rows - which is what the table formats fix.
Four clicks. 1: the row layout fills in, reading by reading. 2: to average the power we sweep through all 18 values. 3: the column layout. 4: jump straight to the kW block - 6 of 18.
Three clicks: dictionary, then run-length, then a codec on top. The numbers underneath are measured live on the sensor readings - written to Parquet in memory just now.
Inside the file: row groups, one chunk per column, and a footer with min/max for every chunk. The reader reads the footer first, skips three of four row groups, reads one chunk out of sixteen.

Delta Lake in one slide. Born at Databricks, open-sourced 2019. The one idea: Parquet files plus a log of commits. It is the format under Databricks and under Fabric's OneLake, so the managed platforms from the last slides are already running on an open format.

Step 1. Creating the table writes no data, only the first log file: protocol and schema. Four panels: the SQL and the commit it writes on top; the files on disk and what a reader sees below (nothing yet).

Step 2. The Parquet file is written first, then one JSON file lists it. Until that commit lands, nobody sees the rows - that is the all-or-nothing guarantee. If the writer crashes before the commit, nothing happened.

Step 3. S1 dropped out at 12:15 and logged a zero. Parquet files can't be edited, so the file holding that row is rewritten without it: remove part-0001, add part-0002. part-0001 stays on disk (struck through), which is what makes time travel work, until VACUUM. Box: deletion vectors, what Databricks and Fabric do instead of rewriting.

Step 4. S2 was miscalibrated. An UPDATE is the same move as the DELETE: rewrite the affected file with the new values, commit remove + add. Four versions now, each one readable. Box: checkpoints - every 10 commits a Parquet snapshot of the whole log, so readers don't replay thousands of JSON files.

The real thing: the full v3 commit delta-rs wrote for the step-4 UPDATE. Three actions. commitInfo is for humans and audit; readVersion is how concurrency works - two writers race to create 00003.json, only one wins, the other checks for conflicts and retries as 00004. add carries min/max stats, so readers skip files from the log alone. remove is a tombstone. protocol and metaData only appear in the first commit, or when they change.

Iceberg gets the same guarantees with a tree instead of a log: catalog -> metadata file -> manifest list (one per snapshot) -> manifests -> Parquet files. A commit is one atomic pointer swap in the catalog. Born at Netflix. Differences on the right; in practice the choice usually follows your platform - Databricks and Fabric speak Delta, Snowflake and AWS lean Iceberg - and they are converging (UniForm; Databricks bought Tabular, the Iceberg founders' company).
Three shapes: a server for the app (Postgres), a library inside your process (DuckDB), a columnar server for real-time analytics (ClickHouse).

Postgres: the default. Most used database in the Stack Overflow survey three years running; extensions make it a geo, vector or time-series database. Show https://db-engines.com/en/ranking if there's time. But it's a row store - remember the Parquet race.
Live: edit the SQL - it runs inside this notebook's Python process, straight on the raw gzipped CSV. Then try SELECT * FROM gold: the dashboard's DataFrame is a table too.
ClickHouse when many users need sub-second dashboards on billions of rows, as data keeps arriving. MergeTree: cheap inserts as small parts, background merges.
Transformation: turning raw into the gold tables a dashboard needs.
Spark for scale - when the data no longer fits one machine. dbt for SQL people - every model a SELECT, ref() builds the DAG, tests and docs come with it.
Serving: where people actually see the data.
The ecosystem as a spectrum: BI apps where you click, dashboards-as-code frameworks, chart libraries, and the new browser-native engines. Left is faster to start, right gives full control.
One example from each project's own gallery - just to show the range. Everything here is free and open source.

Be fair to Power BI: for business self-service, the semantic model and the Microsoft 365 integration it is genuinely hard to beat, and someone else runs it. Open source wins on cost at scale, visual freedom, version control and embedding. Pro is $14/user/month since April 2025; free viewers need F64 capacity.
Superset for data teams - Maxime Beauchemin started it at Airbnb, the same person who started Airflow. Metabase for business users: the easiest thing on this list to get running.

Press play: a D3 bar chart race over the same gold table as the dashboard. Hover a bar, click one to highlight it. You can't build this in a BI tool. It used to cost days of D3; with a coding assistant it is minutes - this one was written with one.

Top: every click is a round trip. Bottom: the engine is compiled to WebAssembly and downloaded once with the data; after that every interaction is local. Perspective, DuckDB-WASM, even Python itself via Pyodide - marimo can export this whole deck to run in the browser.

Live: the fleet's P&L - revenue from the grid settlement, every cost line from finance - pivoted in the browser by Perspective's WASM engine. Open the settings: split by plant or country, switch to a datagrid for a P&L table, filter a year.
Orchestration: something has to run all of this every day, in order, and retry what fails.
Airflow is the safe choice: everybody knows it, every cloud sells it managed. The DAG is Python, the UI shows every task of every run.
Prefect is the fun one: your existing functions plus two decorators, and it runs as a normal script until you want a schedule.
Deployment: where all these tools actually run.

For everyone in the room: an app needs more than its code. Click: Docker packs it all into one box, an image - like a shipping container, the crane doesn't care what's inside. Click: that box runs the same on a laptop, your own servers, any cloud, Kubernetes. That portability is the point - no lock-in to where you run.
Technical detail, skip if needed: our dashboard's Dockerfile is eight lines. Every tool in this talk ships an official image. docker compose runs the whole platform on one machine - often enough.

Four clicks. You declare what should run, Kubernetes places the containers on the machines. A machine dies: its containers restart elsewhere. More users: more dashboard copies. New version: replaced one copy at a time, no downtime.

What it looks like: a Deployment for our own app, Helm charts for Airflow and Superset. Managed Kubernetes exists on every cloud, or k3s/OpenShift on your own servers. Be honest: it's a skill of its own.
The last question of the talk: open source, or a managed platform?
Optional: the trade-off at a glance, before going through it piece by piece.

Cost drivers side by side. Open source: no licences, servers you size, and people - usually the biggest line. Managed: per-user and capacity licences, consumption that grows with every query, egress, fewer engineers but someone watching the bill. And the cost of leaving later. One-liner: open source moves the bill from licences to people; managed moves it from people to usage.

The iceberg. Above the water, the tools - free. Click: to build a platform - deployment, CI/CD, infrastructure as code, scaling. Click: to run it every day - monitoring and on-call, SLAs you now promise yourself, backups and tested restores, security patches and upgrades of every tool. A managed platform does most of this for you; that's what you pay for.

The flip side: that effort buys control. Your versions and roadmap, no forced migrations or price surprises. The best tool for each job instead of one vendor's bundle - and open formats let you swap later. Any feature you need - like the D3 race or the Perspective pivot we saw - without waiting for a vendor.

Who usually goes open source. Organisations with their own infrastructure - data centres, ops teams, data that can't leave. Organisations where data engineering is a core competence and an edge - most of these tools were born there: Airflow and Superset at Airbnb, Iceberg at Netflix, Presto at Facebook. And academia: openness to share and reproduce, tight budgets, own clusters - Postgres and Spark came out of Berkeley, DuckDB out of CWI.
